source: NASA CCMC DONKI - https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/ (real events, 2025-11-14 to 2026-11-14)
setting: Lunar base: only events that reach the Earth-Moon system are included.

fields.dialog: [0] who detected what (real DONKI event + date), [1] explanation of the event type
fields.radiation_points: Extra radiation added to the environment, 0-100 game scale (see radiation_scale)
fields.blackout: True if the event can knock out the base's power
fields.arrival_minutes: Minutes from the robot's warning until the event hits the base
fields.arrival_source: observed (real DONKI times), forecast (NASA model) or estimate (physics/typical value)
fields.chain: Linked events (e.g. flare -> particle storm -> CME). Play them in 'step' order; null = standalone

radiation_scale.FLR: X-ray peak flux, log scale: M1 = 5, X1 = 10, X10 = 15
radiation_scale.SEP: Highest proton energy measured near Earth: >10 MeV = 25, ~30-50 MeV = 40, >100 MeV = 60

blackout_rules.CME: Direct hit at >= 700 km/s: plasma charges the base and electric discharges can trip the power system
blackout_rules.SEP: Only >100 MeV storms: particles cause electronic faults in the power system
blackout_rules.FLR: No: light does not cut power on the Moon

excluded: GST, RBE and MPC only happen inside Earth's magnetic field; CMEs not aimed at Earth; particles and solar wind measured only by STEREO-A (far from the Moon); C-class flares (negligible).

events.name: Solar Flare
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite has detected a class X4.0 solar flare from sunspot region 14274 (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on November 14, 2025).

A solar flare is a sudden, extremely bright flash on the Sun. It happens when twisted magnetic fields above a sunspot snap and reconnect, releasing in minutes more energy than humanity uses in thousands of years. The flash is made of X-rays and ultraviolet light, which travel at the speed of light and reach the Moon in about 8 minutes. On Earth the atmosphere blocks these rays, but the Moon has no air, so they hit the surface directly. Flares are ranked C, M and X, and each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. Big flares are often the first warning of something worse: a storm of fast particles or a coronal mass ejection.
events.arrival_source: observed: minutes from flare start to peak

events.name: Coronal Mass Ejection
dialog: The NASA/ESA SOHO observatory and NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft have detected a coronal mass ejection traveling at 1082 km/s that will hit the Earth-Moon system (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on November 14, 2025).

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.
events.arrival_source: observed: shock measured at Earth

events.name: Solar Energetic Particle Event
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite and the NASA/ESA SOHO observatory have detected a storm of solar protons with energies above 15.8 MeV (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on November 14, 2025).

A solar energetic particle event is a storm of tiny pieces of atoms, mostly protons, that a solar flare or the shock wave of a coronal mass ejection speeds up to almost the speed of light. They can reach the Moon in minutes to a few hours. Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere shield people on the ground, but the Moon has neither, so these particles go through spacesuits, thin walls and the human body, damaging cells and DNA. They also wear out solar panels and can make electronics glitch. It is the most dangerous kind of space weather for astronauts: the best protection is to stay behind thick shielding, like rock, water or heavy equipment, until it passes.
events.arrival_source: observed: minutes after its flare/CME began

events.name: Interplanetary Shock
dialog: NASA's ACE spacecraft and NOAA's DSCOVR satellite have detected a shock wave in the solar wind arriving at Earth and the Moon (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on November 20, 2025).

An interplanetary shock is a sudden wall in the solar wind, the stream of gas that always flows out of the Sun. At the shock, the speed, density and magnetic field of that gas jump all at once, a bit like the sonic boom of a supersonic jet. Most shocks are pushed ahead of a fast coronal mass ejection; others form where fast solar wind crashes into slower wind. When a shock sweeps over the Moon it speeds up nearby particles, adding some radiation, and suddenly changes the electric charge of the lunar surface and of everything standing on it.
events.arrival_source: estimate: typical delay of IPS events in this dataset

events.name: High Speed Solar Wind Stream
dialog: NOAA's DSCOVR satellite and NASA's ACE spacecraft have detected a high speed stream of solar wind (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on November 20, 2025).

A high speed stream is a river of solar wind blowing about twice as fast as usual. It pours out of a coronal hole, a dark region of the Sun where the magnetic field opens into space and lets gas escape freely. Because the Sun rotates once every 27 days, these streams sweep past the Moon like the jet of a rotating garden sprinkler, and the same stream often returns a month later. They are much less violent than other events, but they raise the electric charge of the lunar surface, which makes the fine, sharp moon dust lift and cling to solar panels and equipment.
events.arrival_source: estimate: 1 AU at a typical 650 km/s

It happens when twisted magnetic fields above a sunspot snap and reconnect, releasing in minutes more energy than humanity uses in thousands of years. The flash is made of X-rays and ultraviolet light, which travel at the speed of light and reach the Moon in about 8 minutes. On Earth the atmosphere blocks these rays, but the Moon has no air, so they hit the surface directly. Flares are ranked C, M and X, and each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. Big flares are often the first warning of something worse: a storm of fast particles or a coronal mass ejection.

events.name: High Speed Solar Wind Stream
dialog: NASA's ACE spacecraft and NOAA's DSCOVR satellite have detected a high speed stream of solar wind (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on December 12, 2025).

A high speed stream is a river of solar wind blowing about twice as fast as usual. It pours out of a coronal hole, a dark region of the Sun where the magnetic field opens into space and lets gas escape freely. Because the Sun rotates once every 27 days, these streams sweep past the Moon like the jet of a rotating garden sprinkler, and the same stream often returns a month later. They are much less violent than other events, but they raise the electric charge of the lunar surface, which makes the fine, sharp moon dust lift and cling to solar panels and equipment.
events.arrival_source: estimate: 1 AU at a typical 650 km/s

events.name: Coronal Mass Ejection
dialog: The NASA/ESA SOHO observatory and NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft have detected a coronal mass ejection traveling at 408 km/s that will hit the Earth-Moon system (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on December 22, 2025).

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.

events.name: Interplanetary Shock
dialog: NASA's ACE spacecraft and NOAA's DSCOVR satellite have detected a shock wave in the solar wind arriving at Earth and the Moon (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on January 16, 2026).

An interplanetary shock is a sudden wall in the solar wind, the stream of gas that always flows out of the Sun. At the shock, the speed, density and magnetic field of that gas jump all at once, a bit like the sonic boom of a supersonic jet. Most shocks are pushed ahead of a fast coronal mass ejection; others form where fast solar wind crashes into slower wind. When a shock sweeps over the Moon it speeds up nearby particles, adding some radiation, and suddenly changes the electric charge of the lunar surface and of everything standing on it.

events.name: Solar Energetic Particle Event
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite and the NASA/ESA SOHO observatory have detected a storm of solar protons with energies above 28.2 MeV (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on January 18, 2026).

A solar energetic particle event is a storm of tiny pieces of atoms, mostly protons, that a solar flare or the shock wave of a coronal mass ejection speeds up to almost the speed of light. They can reach the Moon in minutes to a few hours. Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere shield people on the ground, but the Moon has neither, so these particles go through spacesuits, thin walls and the human body, damaging cells and DNA. They also wear out solar panels and can make electronics glitch. It is the most dangerous kind of space weather for astronauts: the best protection is to stay behind thick shielding, like rock, water or heavy equipment, until it passes.

events.name: High Speed Solar Wind Stream
dialog: NOAA's DSCOVR satellite and NASA's ACE spacecraft have detected a high speed stream of solar wind (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on February 5, 2026).

A high speed stream is a river of solar wind blowing about twice as fast as usual. It pours out of a coronal hole, a dark region of the Sun where the magnetic field opens into space and lets gas escape freely. Because the Sun rotates once every 27 days, these streams sweep past the Moon like the jet of a rotating garden sprinkler, and the same stream often returns a month later. They are much less violent than other events, but they raise the electric charge of the lunar surface, which makes the fine, sharp moon dust lift and cling to solar panels and equipment.
events.arrival_source: estimate: 1 AU at a typical 650 km/s

events.name: Coronal Mass Ejection
dialog: The NASA/ESA SOHO observatory and NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft have detected a coronal mass ejection traveling at 394 km/s that will hit the Earth-Moon system (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on February 5, 2026).

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.
events.arrival_source: forecast: NASA WSA-ENLIL model

It happens when twisted magnetic fields above a sunspot snap and reconnect, releasing in minutes more energy than humanity uses in thousands of years. The flash is made of X-rays and ultraviolet light, which travel at the speed of light and reach the Moon in about 8 minutes. On Earth the atmosphere blocks these rays, but the Moon has no air, so they hit the surface directly. Flares are ranked C, M and X, and each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. Big flares are often the first warning of something worse: a storm of fast particles or a coronal mass ejection.

events.name: Coronal Mass Ejection
dialog: NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft and the NASA/ESA SOHO observatory have detected a coronal mass ejection traveling at 236 km/s that will hit the Earth-Moon system (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on April 30, 2026).

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.

events.name: Solar Energetic Particle Event
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite and the NASA/ESA SOHO observatory have detected a storm of solar protons with energies above 28.2 MeV (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on May 25, 2026).

A solar energetic particle event is a storm of tiny pieces of atoms, mostly protons, that a solar flare or the shock wave of a coronal mass ejection speeds up to almost the speed of light. They can reach the Moon in minutes to a few hours. Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere shield people on the ground, but the Moon has neither, so these particles go through spacesuits, thin walls and the human body, damaging cells and DNA. They also wear out solar panels and can make electronics glitch. It is the most dangerous kind of space weather for astronauts: the best protection is to stay behind thick shielding, like rock, water or heavy equipment, until it passes.
events.arrival_source: estimate: typical delay of SEP events in this dataset

events.name: Solar Energetic Particle Event
dialog: NASA's REleASE early-warning system has detected a storm of solar protons with energies above 28.2 MeV (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on June 6, 2026).

A solar energetic particle event is a storm of tiny pieces of atoms, mostly protons, that a solar flare or the shock wave of a coronal mass ejection speeds up to almost the speed of light. They can reach the Moon in minutes to a few hours. Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere shield people on the ground, but the Moon has neither, so these particles go through spacesuits, thin walls and the human body, damaging cells and DNA. They also wear out solar panels and can make electronics glitch. It is the most dangerous kind of space weather for astronauts: the best protection is to stay behind thick shielding, like rock, water or heavy equipment, until it passes.

events.name: Interplanetary Shock
dialog: NOAA's DSCOVR satellite and NASA's ACE spacecraft have detected a shock wave in the solar wind arriving at Earth and the Moon (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on June 11, 2026).

An interplanetary shock is a sudden wall in the solar wind, the stream of gas that always flows out of the Sun. At the shock, the speed, density and magnetic field of that gas jump all at once, a bit like the sonic boom of a supersonic jet. Most shocks are pushed ahead of a fast coronal mass ejection; others form where fast solar wind crashes into slower wind. When a shock sweeps over the Moon it speeds up nearby particles, adding some radiation, and suddenly changes the electric charge of the lunar surface and of everything standing on it.

dialog: NOAA's SOLAR-1 space weather observatory and NASA's IMAP spacecraft have detected a high speed stream of solar wind (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on June 24, 2026).

A high speed stream is a river of solar wind blowing about twice as fast as usual. It pours out of a coronal hole, a dark region of the Sun where the magnetic field opens into space and lets gas escape freely. Because the Sun rotates once every 27 days, these streams sweep past the Moon like the jet of a rotating garden sprinkler, and the same stream often returns a month later. They are much less violent than other events, but they raise the electric charge of the lunar surface, which makes the fine, sharp moon dust lift and cling to solar panels and equipment.

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.
events.arrival_source: forecast: NASA WSA-ENLIL model

events.name: Solar Flare
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite has detected a class M6.3 solar flare from sunspot region 14478 (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on July 3, 2026).

A solar flare is a sudden, extremely bright flash on the Sun. It happens when twisted magnetic fields above a sunspot snap and reconnect, releasing in minutes more energy than humanity uses in thousands of years. The flash is made of X-rays and ultraviolet light, which travel at the speed of light and reach the Moon in about 8 minutes. On Earth the atmosphere blocks these rays, but the Moon has no air, so they hit the surface directly. Flares are ranked C, M and X, and each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. Big flares are often the first warning of something worse: a storm of fast particles or a coronal mass ejection.
events.arrival_source: observed: minutes from flare start to peak

events.name: Coronal Mass Ejection

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. events.name: Interplanetary Shock
dialog: NOAA's SOLAR-1 space weather observatory and NASA's ACE spacecraft have detected a shock wave in the solar wind arriving at Earth and the Moon (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on July 21, 2026).

An interplanetary shock is a sudden wall in the solar wind, the stream of gas that always flows out of the Sun. At the shock, the speed, density and magnetic field of that gas jump all at once, a bit like the sonic boom of a supersonic jet. Most shocks are pushed ahead of a fast coronal mass ejection; others form where fast solar wind crashes into slower wind. When a shock sweeps over the Moon it speeds up nearby particles, adding some radiation, and suddenly changes the electric charge of the lunar surface and of everything standing on it.

events.name: Solar Energetic Particle Event
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite and the NASA/ESA SOHO observatory have detected a storm of solar protons with energies above 100 MeV (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on July 30, 2026).

A solar energetic particle event is a storm of tiny pieces of atoms, mostly protons, that a solar flare or the shock wave of a coronal mass ejection speeds up to almost the speed of light. They can reach the Moon in minutes to a few hours. Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere shield people on the ground, but the Moon has neither, so these particles go through spacesuits, thin walls and the human body, damaging cells and DNA. They also wear out solar panels and can make electronics glitch. It is the most dangerous kind of space weather for astronauts: the best protection is to stay behind thick shielding, like rock, water or heavy equipment, until it passes.
events.arrival_source: observed: minutes after its flare/CME began

A coronal mass ejection is a gigantic cloud of electrically charged gas (plasma) and magnetic field that the Sun throws into space. It can weigh billions of tons and travel at hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second, so it takes about one to four days to cover the 150 million kilometers to the Earth-Moon system. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it, but the Moon has no magnetic field: the plasma hits the surface directly and charges the ground, the base and its equipment with static electricity. Sudden electric discharges can damage circuits and knock out power systems, and the shock wave in front of the cloud can bring extra radiation.
events.arrival_source: forecast: NASA WSA-ENLIL model

events.name: High Speed Solar Wind Stream
dialog: NOAA's SOLAR-1 space weather observatory and NASA's ACE spacecraft have detected a high speed stream of solar wind (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on August 9, 2026).

A high speed stream is a river of solar wind blowing about twice as fast as usual. It pours out of a coronal hole, a dark region of the Sun where the magnetic field opens into space and lets gas escape freely. Because the Sun rotates once every 27 days, these streams sweep past the Moon like the jet of a rotating garden sprinkler, and the same stream often returns a month later. They are much less violent than other events, but they raise the electric charge of the lunar surface, which makes the fine, sharp moon dust lift and cling to solar panels and equipment.
events.arrival_source: estimate: 1 AU at a typical 650 km/s

events.name: Solar Flare
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite has detected a class M1.0 solar flare from sunspot region 14513 (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on August 19, 2026).

A solar flare is a sudden, extremely bright flash on the Sun. It happens when twisted magnetic fields above a sunspot snap and reconnect, releasing in minutes more energy than humanity uses in thousands of years. The flash is made of X-rays and ultraviolet light, which travel at the speed of light and reach the Moon in about 8 minutes. On Earth the atmosphere blocks these rays, but the Moon has no air, so they hit the surface directly. Flares are ranked C, M and X, and each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. Big flares are often the first warning of something worse: a storm of fast particles or a coronal mass ejection.
events.arrival_source: observed: minutes from flare start to peak

events.name: Solar Energetic Particle Event
dialog: NOAA's GOES weather satellite and the NASA/ESA SOHO observatory have detected a storm of solar protons with energies above 100 MeV (based on a real event recorded in NASA's DONKI database on September 5, 2026).

A solar energetic particle event is a storm of tiny pieces of atoms, mostly protons, that a solar flare or the shock wave of a coronal mass ejection speeds up to almost the speed of light. They can reach the Moon in minutes to a few hours. Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere shield people on the ground, but the Moon has neither, so these particles go through spacesuits, thin walls and the human body, damaging cells and DNA. They also wear out solar panels and can make electronics glitch. It is the most dangerous kind of space weather for astronauts: the best protection is to stay behind thick shielding, like rock, water or heavy equipment, until it passes.
events.arrival_source: observed: minutes after its flare/CME began
